Fusion · The Seoul Table

Gochujang Dark Chocolate Tart

Dark chocolate and a measured touch of gochujang, for an unexpected finish.

Korean-French · Medium · Makes one 23 cm tart (10–12 slices)

Jump to recipe ↓

Behind the dish

Lane: fusion — the site's final argument, made in chocolate. Mexican chocolate has known chile for five centuries; this tart is the Korean pantry's entry into that old pairing — a dark chocolate ganache, warm with gochujang's ferment-sweet-heat, in a cocoa-shortbread shell, with the salted sesame finish the tradition brings to its own sweets. The heat arrives after the chocolate, the ferment under the fruit of the cacao, and the first slice converts more skeptics than any savory record on this site. Heat dial: 2 — dessert's ceiling, respectably held.

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • The shell's dough handled like any shortbread: cold and brief. Flour, cocoa, sugar, salt; the butter rubbed to a coarse meal; the yolk and just enough water to clump; pressed into the tart pan, chilled 30 minutes, then blind-baked at 175 °C (15 minutes with weights, 5 without). Cocoa dough tastes raw-flour bitter when underbaked — pull it at the smell of warm brownie, not by color alone.
  • The gochujang whisked into the cream before it meets the chocolate — the paste dissolves completely in warm cream and never in cooling chocolate; the order is the technique, and lumps of paste in set ganache are the recipe's only common failure.

Let’s make it.

  1. 01
    The cream warmed to a bare simmer with the gochujang and the honey, whisked as it warms until the paste fully dissolves and the cream turns a uniform pale-rose tan. Checkpoint — a cooled spoonful tastes of warm cream, honey, and the paste's ferment — gently savory-sweet, no chile burn yet. The cream carries the paste; the chocolate will carry everything.
  2. 02
    The ganache built in three additions: the chopped chocolate in a bowl, the hot gochujang cream poured over and waited on 60 seconds, then stirred from the center outward in slow circles — the emulsion building gradually, the gloss arriving in stages, never whisked to froth. The soft butter and salt stirred in at the gloss. Checkpoint — the ganache is a poured-velvet stream that coats a spatula and holds a light trail — glossy, dark, faintly rose-toned, smelling of chocolate with a warm savory undertone the nose files under "interesting." Frothed or split: it was whisked too hard or the butter was cold; the fix is gentle stirring over a warm water bath until it comes back.
  3. 03
    Poured into the cooled shell, the surface smoothed with a spatula's single pass (more passes leave streaks), and chilled 2 hours to a set that trembles slightly at the pan's tap. Checkpoint — the set's test at the pan's edge: the ganache is firm enough to cut clean and soft enough to melt at the mouth's temperature — the two-hour set, not the overnight brick.
  4. 04
    The finish and the first slice: sesame seeds and flaky salt scattered over the whole surface, the optional gochugaru's faint red dust across one quadrant (the last visual tell — and the table's game of spotting which slices came from the spicy corner). Checkpoint — the eating test, and this record's entire thesis: the first bite reads as an excellent dark chocolate tart — bitter-sweet, silky, the shortbread's cocoa snap. Then, four seconds in, the warmth arrives under the chocolate's finish — not burn, arrival — and the salt and sesame carry it out. The second bite waits for it. The third craves it. That progression is the fusion, complete. Chef’s Note — the dose honesty, because dessert forgives least: this record's dial tops at 2, and the full tablespoon-and-a-half against 250 g of chocolate is the ceiling that keeps the first bite chocolate-first. The buldak instinct to raise it ends the experiment in an edible-but-regrettable place — dessert heat compounds across a whole slice in a way a single noodle-bite never shows you. The tart is the site's last argument and its most disciplined: the whisper, in its most persuasive form.

Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • The shell: blind-baked at 175 °C to warm-brownie smell, cooled fully.
  • The cream: paste fully dissolved in the warm cream, never in the chocolate.
  • The ganache: three-addition emulsion, stirred to velvet, un-frothed.
  • The set: two hours, trembling-firm; the finish: sesame, salt, and the optional corner.

Finish & Plate

Sliced thin — a 23 cm tart serves twelve honestly, because richness like this runs in narrow slices — with espresso or the sikhye register beside. Announce nothing, or announce everything; both servings of the tart have their own kind of party.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Paste lumps in set ganacheDissolved in chocolate, not creamThe cream-dissolve order, always
Ganache split or frothedHard whisking or cold butterGentle re-warm stirring; soft butter
Shell bitter, flouryUnder-baked cocoa doughThe brownie-smell pull, not the clock
Heat arrived too earlyOver-dosed pasteThe full dose is the ceiling; step to 1 tbsp

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Keeps 3 days refrigerated (the ganache's flavor deepens on day two; the shell softens by day three — the second day is the peak). Freezes sliced, a month, thawed cold overnight.
  • Variations: the dial-1 family build; a sesame-praline layer under the ganache; the Mexican acknowledgment done right — a cinnamon thread in the cream beside the paste, the two chile-cultures' hand-shake in one pan.
